newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian parties want June 29 vote, envoy says.
newsitem.headline: Albanian parties want June 29 vote, envoy says.

text.p: International mediator Franz Vranitzky said on Thursday that Albanian political parties had agreed they wanted elections to be held on June 29 but remained divided on the procedure for the vote.
"I think that we have achieved some progress today," Vranitzky, an envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), told reporters.
"I have listened to several parties and the government and they are all of the opinion that the elections should take place on June 29," he said.

He stressed that a consensus still had to be found between parties before a vote was possible. Albanian state news agency ATA quoted Prime Minister Bashkim Fino as saying that no date had been firmly set.

"The elections will take place in June as we decided...the date has not yet been fixed. It will be fixed when there has been an agreement between the political parties and President (Sali) Berisha," he said.
State television read out a statement from Fino appealing for parties to work together for the good of Albania. "This is done by going towards free and fair elections," it said.

Berisha, under pressure when the failure of dodgy investment schemes in which thousands lost their life savings sparked weeks of near-anarchy, agreed last month to an all-party government and to hold elections four years early by the end of June.

Asked at a news conference at the end of his two-day trip whether Berisha could decree the date of the election himself, Vranitzky said: "He consented as everyone else did...When and if there is political consensus in the country it will be 29th."
Vranitzky said the parties were working to narrow the gaps.

"We cannot expect that within a few hours there are binding agreements," he said on his way out of lunch with Tritan Shehu, chairman of Berisha's Democratic Party, and Fatos Nano, chairman of the Socialist Party.
The Socialists were the main opposition until the unity government was formed a month ago.
But Vranitzky added: "I think it was very important that the exponents of Albanian parties agreed they should try everything to find a consensus which is necessary to have a basis for the election."

Vranitzky diplomatically cancelled plans to visit the port of Vlore in the rebel-controlled south after tough talks with Berisha on Wednesday at which the president told him the elections could not go ahead if rebels remained in command.

Vranitzky, who said on Wednesday that he feared the elections were "in some way imperilled" because of differences between parties on how to deal with the rebels, said he had been told Vlore was "not entirely safe".
He said he also thought it was more important to stay in Tirana and press on with talks on the elections.
Parties remained divided over how they viewed the self-proclaimed rebel "committees of national salvation".
"That is certainly the hardest part about the whole election process," Vranitzky said.
He urged the government and rebels on Wednesday to hold "at least a minimum of dialogue" to unblock the situation. Berisha refused: "We are not negotiating with them. No."

Parties are also split on whether to change the voting system which returned Berisha to power with a landslide victory in elections last May that were boycotted by the Socialists and reported by international monitors to contain irregularities.
